entry.title: Nand to Tetris course check in 2026
entry.summary: 2026 checkin of my progress in the nand2tetris course
entry.content:
Introduction

Back in 2017, I started working on a course that intrigued me. The course was called "From Nand To Tetris" (www.nand2tetris.org) and the premise was fairly simple, starting from a primitive NAND gate can I construct a simple computing core on which to run applications written in a high level language. What has prompted me to continue this course after all this time? For one there is a new edition of the book "The Elements of Computing Systems" [TEOCS2] which contains the coursework. I also recently discovered an updated software web application to test my work, contains some upgrades: nifty!

[TEOCS2]Nisan, Noam, and Shimon Schocken. The Elements of Computing Systems. 2nd ed., The MIT Press, 2021.

My progress to now

From my recollection I got stuck on the latter part of the jack compiler frontend, chapter 11 which is code generation. I plan to go into more depth about the compiler frontend in a later blog post. However I did not have an appetite to learn the Jack language properly (I have been spoilt for developer experience from far more mature languages) so I need to get a grip on that before I consider restarting those chapters. In order to ensure I had a good foundation to finish these last project chapters, I wanted check my understanding of the virtual machine was solid and my translation of the virtual machine to assembly was correct (I was more comfortable with the first half of the course given my specialization in computer engineering so I am not planning on repeating that section of the course).

Code Archaeology

Unfortunately, too often when software engineers are working promptly to get through their backlog, they often will put forward thinking and future concerns of readability and maintainability on the backburner. These concerns include code legibility for the poor sod that will end up looking through the codebase (I cannot imagine that the dawn of vibe coding has helped in this matter, but perhaps that will become less urgent if large language models can be taught to stop hallucinating). It should be no surprise that my younger self would not have been thinking about the long term usage of this VM translator given I was hoping to complete the course before graduating.

So let us take a journey, did a soon to be graduate Joshua produce something is that still comprehensible to a far older, more experienced (and jaded) self?

Now one aspect of this to consider is that had completed each project to the satisfaction of completing a chapter, then copied the script into the next chapter if required and started work on this. So I found two scripts named StackTranslator.py in the project folders labelled for chapters 7 and 8. The course recommended that I make a copy of the script I was working on once I had completed chapter 7 upon starting chapter 8. The first script is much simpler than the second so I tested the first with that chapter before moving to the complete chapter.

Good stuff

I am glad to report the good stuff first.

  • The first VM translator was a python script of roughly 450 lines. The second VM translator was a python script of roughly 600 lines. It had no external dependencies so I evidently didn't outsource my thinking and I was sidestepping the concern of distribution that can plague nascent python projects. It was idiomatic enough python 3.6 code that it ran without modification in the latest stable python (3.14).
  • The final script (the second script is considered the final implementation of the VM translator) is separated into classes Parser and Translator. The script can be invoked directly and the script detects this to run the main method that handles argument parsing and running the translator.
  • Running the script without arguments produced a helpful error message. It has a single argument for passing a filepath. Maybe it was overkill to use argparse from the Python standard library for this purpose, but I haven't seen a downside yet and the user experience is just; nicer than anything I would be able to hand roll without getting distracted from the pedagogy of the course.
  • The second script has some handy debugging tools I must have developed as part of working through these chapters. There was a simple method that generated an infinite loop. It's purpose: a poor mans breakpoint 😆 I could add this infinite loop anywhere and run the CPU emulator until hitting it and the systems state would be frozen (program counter notwithstanding). Here is the method:
def epilogue():
  result = []
  result.append("(HW_INFINITE_LOOP)")
  result.append("@HW_INFINITE_LOOP")
  result.append("0;JMP")
  result = "\n".join(result)
  return result

It defines a label @HW_INFINITE_LOOP and immediately jumps to itself unconditionally which ensures that no state in the system changes from the point this assembly is executed. A simple but effective implementation of a software breakpoint for an emulator of the CPU core.

Failure!

Surprisingly the produced assemblies from these scripts did not successfully load into the new nand2tetris web software. This was strange to me because I remembered that I tested the output of these scripts and they had passed before. The current software is a web application which is pretty nifty, but I used the legacy Java software when I completed these chapters. Maybe the new software was slightly different. Let's drill down into the issues.

In chapter 7, this is when we implemented the stack for the virtual machine. There were tests that manipulate the virtual stack directly in order to test my implementation. I generated the assembly file with my stack translator and got an error upon loading the assembly file into the toolchain. Error loading memory: Line 600: Invalid ASM value: M+D. Did you mean D+M? I was quite surprised because I thought I recalled completing these chapters without seeing this error before. This seems to be a straightforward fatal error that prevent the tests to even run. Investigating further it appears that when I emitted certain addition instructions I did not consistently have the same order in the emitted instruction than the specification. The early emulator was less strict and allowed these instructions and treated them identically (addition is commutative after all). Ensuring that all addition instructions emitted from my solution used the correct operand order fixed this issue.

I cleared the test output from the chapter 8 and regenerated it using the StackTranslator.py script that I found there. There was no errors and the script dutifully produced an assembly file for the FibonacciSeries test vm file. Loading it into the new generation of the nand2tetris tools produced this error: Error loading memory: Line 69: expected "JMP", "JLE", "JNE", "JLT", "JGE", "JEQ", or "JGT" navigating to the offending line in the produced assembly file. 0; JMP which was confusing to say the least, the command is clearly a JMP command. My only theory at the point was that the emulator was objecting to the formatting of the assembly file which was correct. Removing the space between the semicolon and jump instruction fixed this issue .eg 0;JMP (updating the stack translator to produce this formatting from now on in all jump instructions which a simple case of find and replace).

Fixing the formatting of the jump instructions led to the assembly files loading successfully into the emulator. Nice! The course provides a domain specific language of setting up the emulator and running it, which is used to great effect to run tests of our project. I found that when I ran the emulator using the provided test script, the result did not match the expected result. There was a problem in the generated assembly that meant that certain tests were clearly failing despite my recollection that my solution did pass these tests before. After investigating it, I discovered the issue by reading the chapter in the course book again and discovered that some of the tests required me to generate a bootstrap to run the test and others did not. The test I was studying did not need this bootstrap and sure enough, omitting the bootstrap invocation in my translator caused the test to pass again (thankfully I had clearly labelled the method that generated the bootstrap so I could comment it out easily). I had ascertained that I had a working VM implementation in my project work.

Resolution Takeaways

Always use source control

It was so frustrating that I did not version control my attempts! It would have been much easier to determine the progression of the development of the code I would have clearly seen that the were changes required to pass certain tests without having to dredge through the coursebook again! I would have also been able to change between versions of the solution at my leisure so I could more quickly test each stage of my scripts in development.

Document expectations

It is hard to know what you are taking for granted when you embark on a software solution, it is something that can only come with experience. I expect this to be a continuing source of friction people will encounter when using large language models as well, as unconscious expectations will not be communicated the agent will take a reasonable but undesirable path which will be overlooked by the operator. For example, not leaking all the source code when deploying to production (common sense is still mostly a human concept, for now even if we choose not to exercise it!). If I had added a couple targeted comments in certain locations in my solution explaining when to use the bootstrap, it would have saved me half an hour.

Debugging

It is possible to diagnose and resolve issues in legacy code regardless of how underdocumented it is but there is a penalty in terms of time to rework as it will take longer for an unfamiliar developer to get acquainted with the code. I was able to take some heuristics in my debugging journey because I had some latent knowledge of the implementation and even vague recollections can help start the problem solving process in the right direction, but without these sometimes you have to trace the execution of a program at a low level just to identify the fault in the system.

Next steps

Now I am convinced I have completed chapters 7 and 8, next is to tackle using the Jack language itself and unearth my first attempt at the frontend code generation I abandoned previously. This is chapter 9 and my aim to make something relatively meaty with this language so I can understand it further. The main issue I had with this part was lacking some programmer comforts that I am used to in far more mature languages and some small friction with the toolchain, as well as life getting in the way. I was also concerned that my implementation of the virtual machine was not particularly efficient (a concern I still hold and would like to dedicate some time to confirm and resolving that). Once I am happy with my grasp of the Jack language, I want to revisit what I had done with the compiler frontend so far and (probably) rewrite it in order to complete the course to my satisfaction.

entry.title: How to save website form data
entry.summary: How to save entered form data on a website
entry.content:
I want it to be simple

Continuing in my pattern of attempting things that seem simple at first, but turn into a rabbit hole. I was filling out a (single page) web form that was quite long and I needed to pause my progress, I wanted to capture my responses so that if accidently closed the page, I didn't lose my responses. Also I thought it would be good forward planning to keep a copy of my responses myself.

Of course, it is possible to copy and paste each response individually, but this is exactly the sort of repetitive toil I try to excise from my life.

The Initial Attempt

Sometimes the simplest solution works so we will try it. To select all page elements, the shortcut Ctrl+A works in many circumstances. Using the shortcut on our completed form, we want to see whether the input is also selected.

Unfortunately, this approach doesn't work as it only selects elements of the form itself and doesn't include my responses.

Autofilled forms?

Firefox and Chrome support autofill of forms for certain fields of the form which is great for repeated entry of your address etc. This usage is slightly different than what I wanted because I want to save all fields in a given form I am currently filling out, including fields that have never been seen before.

Extensions?

There are extensions which improve the experience of filling in longer forms, the main one I am aware of is Form History Control.

Copying the HTML

Let us look at the options for us built-in to the browser. These options both use the Developer Tools.

After I thought about why this happening, it made sense to me pretty quickly that copying the HTML markup was not going to return my responses. HTML is a markup language which defines the structure of webpages, it really doesn't concern itself with the interactivity of the webpage when it is being displayed by the web browser. We need to find a way to access the document as it is being presented by the browser.

Accessing the DOM

We can also access the DOM (Document Object Model) using the Developer Tools. It is an interface that lends itself to accessing the data of the objects that are present in the webpage as it being displayed. I created a small Javascript snippet that returns the contents of all input fields of selected element kinds.

  • <input> elements need to be selected as most user input occurs in them
  • <textarea> elements can be writable so we should grab their contents
  • <select> elements need to be included as dropdown selections use them
const formFields = document.querySelectorAll('input, textarea, select');
const fieldData = [];
formFields.forEach(field => {
  fieldData.push({
    name: field.name,
    value: field.value,
    autoname: field.attributes['autocomplete']
    });
});
var newWindow = window.open();
const formatted = fieldData.map(obj => JSON.stringify(obj)).join('\n');
newWindow.document.write('<pre>' + formatted + '</pre>'); })();

I have tested this code snippets with standard HTML forms as , then I tested it with some forms created in Google Forms as that is very popular. The form that trigger this inquiry was actually created by Cognito, I hadn't heard about this company before. It presented some problems with my first attempt at this code; the name attribute of the final output objects were not defined. I eventually found that there is an autocomplete attribute that contained the name of the given field so I simply included that in the dump as well.

Now we have Javascript code that accesses the DOM to get the content of input fields in a good variety of cases, how do we package it for easy usage?

Bookmarklets

A bookmarklet is a Javascript script that can run on click, similar to how a normal bookmark will trigger the browser to load the linked website.

Overall, it is a great idea. Once I have my code snippet inside the URI for the bookmarklet, it will open a new window with the list of objects (map containing the name, value and autocomplete) of the selected fields printed. The only thing I can complain about is that the entry for the bookmark URI is not designed to handle multiline input (because most bookmarket targets are usually a single line URL of course) so the developer UX leaves a lot to be desired.

Conclusion

Although, I could definitely improve the accessibility of using my bookmarklet (the output format of the form response dump is a bit ugly), I decided I was happy enough with the outcome of this exercise. I now get a simple dump of the name of the input elements along with their contents.

Some improvements I could envision myself making:

  • Iterating over the document top to bottom, dumping all HTML content alongside the field contents
  • Pretty printing the field data objects
  • Adding more metadata in the field data objects .eg types

entry.title: How to make a static site with Pelican
entry.summary: Article about publishing (& troubleshooting) a static blog with Pelican
entry.content:
Setup

Following the document to install pelican was straightforward.

In order to install pelican without disturbing the python installation provided by the system packages I made use of virtualenv. Once I have my virtualenv set up I am free to install any packages that I need through pip inside that virtual environment without disrupting my system. The essentials of virtualenvs are explained well here https://pycon.switowski.com/02-packages/virtualenv/.

Installing pelican did not pose any problems nor did initialising the project for my blog.

Theming

Pelican supports theming from a community managed selection of themes, there is a live preview available at https://pelicanthemes.com/. The docs describe the tool used to install themes for pelican was installed with the pip package and it is called pelican-themes. I cloned the repository of the community managed themes and browsed the preview website for a theme that I wanted to use on my blog. I first settled on 'water-iris', what won me over was the ASCII art for the title and the icons for the social links.

Troubleshooting Theming

After I had installed the 'water-iris' theme, I wanted to run the live preview with this theme to test it out. There is a settings file in the project root called 'pelicanconf.py' which includes a setting of which theme to apply to the published blog. One of the options during the project initialisation was to include a Makefile and there is a 'make devserver' target provided that enables auto reload on file changes within the blog project. Once the site had started serving, I opened my browser to see this:

Clearly, there was something wrong with the application of the theme to my blog. I got a bit stuck at this point and thought maybe I had done something wrong in the configuration of the pelican settings or project directory structure. While I was exploring possibilities and troubleshooting the issue, I eventually examined the pelican-themes repo I had cloned and found out that the folder was empty. That would definitely explain this strange behaviour, but why was there nothing in this directory? When I looked again at the GitHub repo for the pelican-themes repo I realized that the water-iris theme was included as a git submodule. When I had cloned the repository, I had forgotten to add the flags that would recursively clone all the submodules contained within. Running git submodule update --init --recursive in the pelican-themes working directory and then reinstalling the theme resolved this issue.

Troubleshooting Theming Again!

Now that I had theming working on my blog, I wanted to change the theme especially the title ASCII art as I wanted it to say my name. pelican-themes supports installing the theme folder as a symbolic link instead of a copy which facilitates theme development. I used the command pelican-themes -s ../pelican-themes/water-iris/ --verbose to install the theme as a symbolic link so I could make changes to the theme. The command completed successfully so I reran the devserver make target. I got this perplexing error Exception: Could not find the theme water-iris and indeed if I listed the installed themes with pelican-themes -l the 'water-iris' theme was absent as well.

So I started troubleshooting again, I was suspicious that the theme was not listed at all despite the others being listed so I examined the symlink created by the tool (the --verbose flag came in handy). I ran file on the symlink and got this output in response.

/home/jachermann/.pyenv/versions/pelican/lib/python3.11/site-packages/pelican/themes/water-iris: broken symbolic link to ../pelican-themes/water-iris/

The issue was caused by the relative path I passed into the tool and it is resolved from the location of the created symlink rather than from my working directory, this is a known issue with pelican-themes but the pull request to fix this issue was closed without being merged. Either this pull request should be reopened or the argument documentation should be updated to highlight that the path passed in must the absolute path, additionally it would be great to update the list option to display broken symbolic links rather than leaving them absent. Passing in the absolute path of the 'water-iris' theme folder when using the -s option with the pelican-themes tool resolved this issue.

Awesome ASCII art

I was inspired to investigate generating an ASCII art title for my blog and found pyfiglet which is a python port of the figlet terminal program which can generate ASCII art. I installed pyfiglet into the virtualenv I am using to install all dependencies required for my blog. I wanted to get a sample of every type of font that is provided by the package by default, fortunately as Python as a very dynamic programming language, it is simple to investigate the imported module and find the list of fonts.

jachermann@localhost[my_blog_source]> python

>>> dir(pyfiglet)
['COLOR_CODES', 'CharNotPrinted', 'DEFAULT_FONT', 'Figlet', 'FigletBuilder', 'FigletError', 'FigletFont', 'FigletProduct', 'FigletRenderingEngine', 'FigletStr

zipfile']
>>> f = pyfiglet.Figlet()

Once we have the list of fonts, it is trivial to generate a text file listing each font and sample text in that font.

with open('figlets.txt', 'w') as figlets:
  for font in fonts:
    figlets.write(font)
    figlets.write('\n')
    tmpf = pyfiglet.Figlet(font=font)
    figlets.write(tmpf.renderText('Joshua'))
    figlets.write('\n')

Adding my custom title

I have been composing this first post as I have established this blog, in the end, I decided to opt for a different theme then the one I spent so long diagnosing.

Once I had selected my choice of font for the title, I had to make changes to the theme to add it to the site header. This is because the blog content is only responsible for the static content of posts and pages rather than the look of the site itself. I moved the theme folder I had chosen into my blog source repository and installed it via symbolic link with pelican-themes. Then I could edit the HTML templates provided by the theme to add my custom title and keep my changes in version control.

Jinja templating is used to pass parameters from the blog content to the theme, I wanted to see if I could add my bespoke parameter for passing the title word art I had selected. Configuration used by pelican is set in 'pelicanconf.py' and that includes configuration for the theme as well. It is just a python file so I added the follow code alongside the generated configuration. Here is the relevant snippet:

from pyfiglet import Figlet
figlet = Figlet(font='ansi_shadow')

# custom settings are prefaced with CUSTOM_

AUTHOR = 'Joshua Achermann'
SITENAME = 'Joshua Achermann'
CUSTOM_TITLE = figlet.renderText(SITENAME)

This allows me to use the value in the template for the title , this theme has it in an include called 'jumbotron.html'. The file is small enough to include in full. I added a condition that checks for the presence of my custom parameter 'CUSTOM_TITLE' and includes a pre formatted section to display it. If the custom parameter is not present, it falls back to its original behaviour of including the site name variable directly.

<div class="jumbotron" id="overview">
  <div class="container">
      {% if CUSTOM_TITLE %}
      <pre aria-hidden="true">{{ CUSTOM_TITLE }}</pre>
      {% else %}
      {{ SITENAME }}
      {% endif %}
      {% if SITESUBTITLE %}
  <p class="lead">{{ SITESUBTITLE }}</p>
      {% endif %}
  </div>
</div>

Creating posts

Pelican supports markup languages reStructedText and Markdown for writing blog articles, others may be supported through plugins but I wanted to stick to the well trodden paths so I would choose between these two. I had used Markdown before (many README files are composed in Markdown) and liked it quite a lot, but I decided to write my blog entries in reStructedText (rst) in order to learn it properly as it is used extensively in Python documentation. This very post was crafted in a rst file (very meta I am aware). All blog content including static resources are stored in a subfolder called 'content', itself containing other subfolders such as 'images' or 'pages'. This directory structure can be changed but 'pelicanconf.py' contains settings that need to be updated to reflect these changes. In my setup, there is a content subfolder called 'posts' which will contain all the blog article rst files.

Publishing to GitHub Pages

I followed the instructions on this page https://pages.github.com/ to create a repo for my GitHub Page and then followed the instructions in the publishing a project site to GitHub Pages from a Branch to publish to it.

The first time you are going to publish you need to enable the GitHub Page setting in the repository settings as described here.

entry.title: How to install all my GOG games
entry.summary: A journey to bulk install some games
entry.content:
Subject Matter

Steam and GOG (Good Old Games) are online stores for purchasing video games which can be downloaded (it all happens digitally these days).

I recently purchased an excess of storage for my main computer (four 2TB SSDs) and wanted to make use of it by installing a good chunk of the games from my Steam library. When the Library tab of the Steam client is selected, your list of games is presented by name and small icon on the left side. Selecting games in bulk is easily achieved by holding the Shift key and selecting each game on the list, then you can right click on a selected item to bring up a context menu including actions to perform in bulk (installation being one of them).

Furthermore, games can be easily sorted into categories. Overall, the user experience was very pleasant and I had setup the queue of games to be installed very quickly. Even with so much storage, I had to be selective about which Steam games I installed (Steam sales are my weakness). I don't need to be so cautious with my collection of GOG games as there are less of them and they don't use as much storage per game. I aimed to install all of my GOG games on a single 2TB drive, I felt this should be a simple task.

Problem

Similarly to how Steam provides a client to install and manage your game collection, GOG has provided their own client. It is called GOG Galaxy and it looks pretty slick with a polished purple aesthetic. By default, the games are presented visually as rows of products on shelves but this can be changed to a more traditional list view which I prefer.

Unfortunately, I discovered there is no way to select games in bulk in the GOG Galaxy client. If I wanted to install all my games, I would need to click the install button on each game entry, then click again in each dialog to confirm the installation. This would result in hundreds of mouse clicks when really I wanted a single mouse click to install ALL games, this possibility was not even present with my Steam bulk installation as I couldn't install each and every game.

After determining that this feature is not present in the GOG Galaxy client, I decided to explore other possibilities.

Direct Downloads

Galaxy was not always provided by GOG and before it existed, the way to download and manage your games was on the GOG website. You can download the installers from here and run them on your computer. Someone has built a python script to bulk download direct installers and additional content from the GOG website, which would probably be the best option for what I want.

The reason I didn't go with this option is because I stubbornly wanted to install the games with GOG Galaxy integration.

Alternate Clients

GOG Galaxy does not have native Linux support. If you want to manage your GOG games on a Linux system, your best bet is to use Lutris. My main computer is running Windows 10 and there are alternative game launcher clients that run on Windows: Heroic and Playnite.

I thought maybe one of these alternative clients might support bulk installation but unfortunately even though they let you select multiple games simultaneously they don't let you install them in bulk. I started to consider making changes to these launchers to add this feature as they are both open source but the thought of learning a new codebase I am unfamiliar with is daunting. There had to be an easier way.

Automation the Lazy Way

I decided to use AutoHotkey in order to automate the process. Using Playnite, I connected it to my GOG account and it downloaded all the metadata for my games. Then it presented me the list of all my GOG games, with which I could craft a script to repeatedly press down and enter to start installing each game.

#Persistent
SetTimer, PressKeys, 1000
return

PressKeys:
Send, {Down}
Sleep, 100
Send, {Enter}
return

Esc::ExitApp

That last line is very important as it allows me to cease the script once it has reached the bottom of the list by pressing the Escape key. Not quite pressing a single button, but once you set it up and run it, it will work for any number of games. At least that is what I hoped...

Performance Issues

Once the game has been selected in Playnite, it does eventually appear in the GOG Galaxy download queue exactly as I intended. The problem is that when the download queue started to expand to a size of about 300, the client really started to struggle.

The client would take a long time to even show the Downloads entry in the menu upon starting up. It is hard to say why the program struggled so much without having access to the source code, however I rummaged around in the configuration files to see if there was some clues. I figured out that the client uses sqlite to store its job queue. It is not encrypted and can be explored easily using a tool like DB Browser. Sometimes the stalls could be fixed by clearing the job queue (there is a jobs table that can be cleared with a simple SQL TRUNCATE statement) or even deleting the jobs database file completely, but mostly it was a waiting game.

Another problem is that some installers that run through the GOG Galaxy are not fully quiet and require user interaction in order to continue so I needed to check it regularly.

After a long wait over 4 days, checking and restarting the GOG Galaxy client each time it stalled. I eventually installed every GOG game. After trimming down and removing some duplicate games I ended up with 492 installed GOG games which took up 845 GB on my drive.

Conclusion

Ultimately, I achieved the outcome that I wanted although it was far more time consuming than I expected it to be. I went down some rabbit holes but found a solution that is reasonably simple but flawed. As of the time of writing, Steam really is the most featureful client out of any proprietary game launcher and that is no doubt playing massively into its success. I have found that other game launchers are missing features I expect as standard because they are present in Steam, fortunately there are open source game launchers that the community could rally around to reach parity with Steam.
